deep.reconstruction:
Context: bundle R.Minimal holds Riemann's notes on his minimal-surface memoir, which K. Hattendorff edited and published in 1867. On the preceding page Riemann addresses a 'Sie' and comments on a draft. The next page contains Hattendorff's reply ('Ich erlaube mir hierneben vorzulegen, was ich heute Morgen ausgearbeitet habe ...'). So this page is Riemann's critique, in points I–III, of Hattendorff's write-up.

I (end of the 'remarks on the general formula'). The surface is locally a graph x = x(y,z). The unit normal is (cos r, sin r cos phi, sin r sin phi), where phi is the theta of the previous page. In the first variation of area, ∬ dy dz/|cos r| varied by δx, Riemann wants the integration to run over the whole surface. He notes this requires that the boundary term produced by integration by parts varies continuously over the whole surface, including the curve where cos r = 0. That term is sin r cos phi δx dz ± sin r sin phi δx dy.

He then turns to general parameters p, q, which must take each value pair at most once on the surface. One may choose p (the transcription has f) so that p = 0 on the boundary and p has a single interior maximum. The level curves of p are then closed curves shrinking to a point, and q is an angle-like coordinate running round them. Under the integral sign stands a functional determinant (Jacobian):

∬ (f_p g_q − f_q g_p) dp dq = ∬ [∂(f g_q)/∂p − ∂(f g_p)/∂q] dp dq = ∬ [∂(g f_p)/∂q − ∂(g f_q)/∂p] dp dq.

[My fill-in:]
- The ∂/∂q-terms integrate to zero, because q is periodic along each closed level curve.
- The ∂/∂p-terms integrate to boundary values. At the interior maximum the q-curve degenerates to a point and contributes nothing.
- Hence the integral equals ∮ f (∂g/∂q) dq, or equivalently −∮ g (∂f/∂q) dq. Both run over the whole boundary in the positive sense; the two agree by integration by parts along a closed curve.

He adds that this holds also for complex f, g. In modern terms: ∬ df∧dg = ∮ f dg = −∮ g df (Green/Stokes in parameter form).

II. A simplification of Hattendorff's computation. Let s = y + iz and s' = y − iz. Let t be the harmonic conjugate of x on the surface. Let η, η' be the stereographic coordinates of the normal: η = tan(r/2) e^{iφ}, η' = tan(r/2) e^{−iφ}. The defining relations are

2 ds + (dx + i dt)/η' − η (dx − i dt) = 0,
2 ds' − η'(dx + i dt) + (dx − i dt)/η = 0.

Set (implicitly) X = x − ti and X' = x + ti. The relations become

2ds − η dX + dX'/η' = 0,
2ds' + dX/η − η' dX' = 0.

Treat X, X' as independent. Then 2 s_X = η, 2 s_X' = −1/η', 2 s'_X = −1/η and 2 s'_X' = η'. Equality of mixed partials gives

(1/η'^2) ∂η'/∂X = ∂η/∂X',
(1/η^2) ∂η/∂X' = ∂η'/∂X.

Substituting one into the other gives (1 − 1/(ηη')^2) ∂η/∂X' = 0. Riemann concludes ∂η/∂X' = 0 and ∂η'/∂X = 0. So η depends on X alone and η' on X' alone. Inverting, X is a function of η alone and X' of η' alone. Hence

2ds = η (dX/dη) dη − (1/η')(dX'/dη') dη',
2ds' = −(1/η)(dX/dη) dη + η'(dX'/dη') dη'.

These give s and s' by quadratures in η, η'. Together with dX = (dX/dη) dη this is Riemann's form of the Weierstrass–Enneper representation, with the single free function X(η) (and its conjugate).

III. Hattendorff's formulas for changing the coordinate system cover only an arbitrary choice of the x-axis, i.e. of the pole of the stereographic map. Riemann says this suffices for all applications and should be left as is. If an arbitrary rotation about the x-axis is also wanted, one needs (continued on the next page) η1 = e^{iθ}(η − α)/(1 + α'η). This is the general rotation of the sphere written as a unitary Möbius transformation of the stereographic coordinate.
errors: The step from the two integrability conditions to ∂η/∂X' = 0 divides by 1 − 1/(ηη')^2, i.e. assumes ηη' ≠ 1. Since ηη' = tan^2(r/2), the excluded case ηη' = 1 is r = π/2, cos r = 0 identically: the normal is everywhere perpendicular to the x-axis. That is the cylindrical/planar case parallel to x, and Riemann does not mention it. Fittingly, it is the same cos r = 0 degeneracy flagged in part I.
Treating X = x − ti and X' = x + ti as independent variables is formal, since they are complex conjugates. It is standard and justified by analyticity, but tacit here.
The identification X = x − ti, X' = x + ti, needed to pass from the dx ± i dt form to the dX, dX' form, is not stated. Note the conjugation convention: X goes with dx − i dt.

Part I: the sign between sin r cos φ δx dz and sin r sin φ δx dy depends on the boundary orientation. From x_y dz − x_z dy one expects the relative sign to be minus, so the '+' read in the transcription may be a misreading or an orientation convention.

Part I: the claim that the Jacobian integral reduces to ∮ f g_q dq tacitly assumes f, g are smooth at the interior maximum of p, where the (p,q) coordinates are singular. Otherwise the inner boundary term need not vanish. This is acceptable as written, but implicit.

results.what: Integral of a Jacobian determinant over a region parametrized by (p,q), with p = 0 on the boundary and a single interior maximum, reduces to the boundary integral ∮ f ∂g/∂q dq = −∮ g ∂f/∂q dq, valid also for complex f, g.
results.modern_name: Green's theorem / Stokes' theorem for ∬ df∧dg = ∮ f dg

results.what: Continuity requirement on the boundary term of the first variation of area across the curve where cos r = 0, so the variation can be integrated over the whole surface rather than over graph pieces.
results.modern_name: First variation of area; global (parametric) treatment versus graph representation
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760) for the minimal surface equation; global parametric treatment standard

results.what: From the relations 2ds = η dX − dX'/η' etc., the integrability conditions force η = η(X) and η' = η'(X'). Hence s and s' are given by quadratures in η, η' with one arbitrary function X(η).
results.modern_name: Weierstrass–Enneper representation of minimal surfaces (Riemann's version via the stereographic Gauss map)
results.usually_credited_to: Enneper (1864), Weierstrass (1866); Riemann's version published posthumously by Hattendorff (1867)

results.what: Change of coordinates: rotations of the sphere act on the stereographic normal coordinate η by η1 = e^{iθ}(η − α)/(1 + α'η).
results.modern_name: SU(2)/SO(3) acting by unitary Möbius transformations on the Riemann sphere

deep.surprise_reason: The page belongs to Riemann's correspondence with Hattendorff over the posthumously published minimal-surface memoir (1867). The Weierstrass–Enneper-type reduction, the Green/Stokes boundary formula and the Möbius rotation formula all appear in, or underlie, that published paper and are already attributed to Riemann. The value is editorial: it shows how Riemann shaped the derivation, including a slicker integrability argument. There is no new mathematics.

transcription_corrections: 'so annehmen daß f in der Begrenzung 0 ist': the image reads 'p' (the parameter p is chosen to vanish on the boundary and have one interior maximum), not f. The preceding '[?] [?]' is likely 'p so'.
'eine Lagrange'sche[?]' at the line end is doubtful; the sense is 'Hat man dann unter dem Integralzeichen eine Functionaldeterminante'.
'der mit dem Integral fortschreitende Theil' is probably 'heraustretende Theil' (the boundary term that comes out of the integral).

The term 'sin r cos φ δx dz + sin φ δx dy' should probably be read as sin r cos φ δx dz ± sin r sin φ δx dy. The struck-out 'sin r' appears to be rewritten, and the sign should be checked against the image.
In III, 'wenn {+die+} x Axe oder der Pol beliebig gewählt werden soll' fits the image; '[?] bei' is likely 'was bei'.
The first line '[?]nalmass[?]' is probably 'normalmäßig' or similar; uncertain.
